atp.short: The molecule whose splitting (hydrolysis) to ADP and phosphate powers muscle contraction and ion pumps. The only energy currency muscle spends directly.

adp.short: What is left of ATP after one phosphate is split off. Rising ADP is a signal that drives ATP resynthesis.

hydrolysis.short: Splitting a molecule with water. ATP hydrolysis (ATP + H₂O → ADP + Pi) releases the energy muscles use.

glycolysis.short: Breakdown of glucose or glycogen to pyruvate in the cytosol, making ATP fast without oxygen. Some pyruvate always becomes lactate; more does when it is made faster than the mitochondria take it up.

oxidative-phosphorylation.short: ATP made in mitochondria using oxygen, from carbohydrate and fat. Slowest maximal rate of the three routes, but almost unlimited capacity.

sarcolemma.short: The cell membrane of a muscle fibre. It carries the electrical signal along the fibre and holds the transporters and pumps that move glucose and ions in and out.

cytosol.short: The watery fluid inside a cell, outside the organelles. Glycolysis and many other reactions happen here; in muscle it is also called the sarcoplasm.

mitochondria.short: The structures in the cell where the Krebs cycle, beta-oxidation and the electron transport chain run, using oxygen to make most of the ATP.

sarcoplasmic-reticulum.short: A network of membrane sacs wrapped around the contractile filaments of a muscle fibre. It stores Ca²⁺, releases it to start contraction and pumps it back (using ATP) to relax.

myonucleus.short: One of the many nuclei in a muscle fibre. Each holds the full DNA and controls protein making in the stretch of fibre around it.

organelle.short: A structure with its own job inside a cell, often wrapped in membrane: the nucleus, mitochondria and sarcoplasmic reticulum are examples.

glycogen.short: The stored form of glucose: long branched chains kept in muscle and liver. Muscle glycogen is the main carbohydrate fuel in hard exercise.

triglyceride.short: The storage form of fat: three fatty acids joined to glycerol. Kept mainly in adipose tissue, with a smaller store inside muscle fibres (IMTG).

fatty-acid.short: A long chain of carbon atoms with an acid group at one end. Split off triglycerides and burned in mitochondria for ATP.

amino-acid.short: The building block of proteins (20 kinds). The body has no store of protein kept for fuel; amino acids supply only a few % of the energy in exercise.

imtg.short: Fat stored as droplets inside muscle fibres, close to the mitochondria. A fuel alongside fatty acids delivered by the blood from adipose tissue.

coupled-reaction.short: A reaction that would not go on its own (it needs energy) driven by linking it to one that releases energy, usually ATP hydrolysis.

enzyme.short: A protein that speeds up one chemical reaction without being used up. Almost every step of energy metabolism has its own enzyme.

substrate.short: The molecule an enzyme acts on. Glycogen is the substrate of glycogen phosphorylase.

km.short: The substrate concentration at which an enzyme works at half its top rate (Vmax). Low Km: the enzyme is near full speed even at low substrate.

allosteric.short: Control of an enzyme by a molecule that binds away from the active site and makes it faster or slower. AMP speeds up glycogen phosphorylase this way; ADP and AMP speed up PFK.

phosphorylation.short: Adding a phosphate group to a molecule. On an enzyme it acts as an on/off switch: adrenaline signalling phosphorylates glycogen phosphorylase and turns it on.

rate-limiting-step.short: The slowest, most controlled step of a pathway. Its enzyme sets the speed of the whole pathway; PFK plays this role in glycolysis.

pfk.short: The main control enzyme of glycolysis. Sped up by ADP, AMP and Pi when ATP demand rises; slowed by H⁺ in the test tube.

glycogen-phosphorylase.short: The enzyme that breaks glucose units off glycogen, using phosphate (Pi) as its second substrate. Turned on by Ca²⁺ and adrenaline (phosphorylation) and sped up by AMP.

diffusion.short: Net movement of molecules from high to low concentration by random motion. It costs no ATP and can only go downhill.

glut4.short: The glucose transporter of muscle and fat cells. Insulin and muscle contraction move it from inside the fibre to the membrane, so more glucose can enter.

na-k-atpase.short: A membrane pump that uses one ATP to move 3 Na⁺ out of the cell and 2 K⁺ in, restoring the gradients that nerve and muscle signals run down.

membrane-potential.short: The voltage across a cell membrane, inside negative: about −80 to −90 mV in resting human skeletal muscle. Set mainly by the K⁺ gradient.

action-potential.short: A brief electrical signal that runs along a nerve or muscle membrane: Na⁺ rushes in, then K⁺ flows out. It tells the muscle fibre to contract.

catabolism.short: Breaking larger molecules (glycogen, fat, protein) down into smaller ones. Releases energy, part of which is captured by rebuilding ATP.

anabolism.short: Building larger molecules (glycogen, proteins, new mitochondria) from smaller ones. Needs energy, paid for with ATP.
